It doesn't even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon." Zoom out: Trump also made a broader case for the war, saying many…

33e1d7779a:610028401a6d1944.title: Love is pricey. Here's what young Americans are doing about it
33e1d7779a:610028401a6d1944.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:610028401a6d1944.summary: Data: Zelle New Economics of Dating Report; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Rising costs are changing dating for more than eight in 10 Gen Z and millennial daters, leaving some to stop courting altogether, per new data from Zelle. The big picture: Young Americans are pushing off milestones under cost pressures — and the milestones themselves , from getting hitched to buying a home, are getting pricier once they get there. Driving the news: For younger Americans, just planning a date is a costly ordeal, with 17% of active Gen Z and Millennial daters saying they've gone into debt trying to maintain the dating lifestyle. Nearly one-third say they've gone on fewer dates amid rising costs. A smaller share, 11%, say they've stopped dating because they couldn't afford it. Members of Gen Z are more likely to split the cost of a date because of rising costs (26%) than Millennials (18%). Daters have changed strategies to lighten the cost burden — like suggesting free activities and spending more time on dates at home, which were used by 37% and 33% of active daters, respectively. The intrigue: As costs weigh on younger Americans, perhaps it's unsurprising that checkbook chemistry plays a big role in their love stories: Half of active daters say financial compatibility has at some point mattered more than romantic chemistry when deciding to keep dating someone. Men are more likely to say that than women (56% versus 45%), as are Gen Zers (53%) than Millennials (46%). But be warned: Talking money too much can kill the mood. For example, complaining about the price of everything or chatting too much about income would both give 47% of daters the "ick." What they're saying: "Dating has always come with unspoken rules, but rising costs are forcing a rewrite," Denise Leonhard, general manager of Zelle, said in a statement. "Financial compatibility is becoming part of the chemistry test. The new flex isn't running up the tab; it's reading the room, respecting the budget and showing…

33e1d7779a:5ef0dec5e13d0320.title: A GOP senator wants Trump Jr. subpoenaed after Russian oligarch-funded wedding
33e1d7779a:5ef0dec5e13d0320.author: Andrew Pantazi
33e1d7779a:5ef0dec5e13d0320.summary: Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) is urging Senate Judiciary leaders to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden to investigate whether presidential family ties have been used for private family gain. Why it matters: The Republican Curtis is pressing a Republican-led Senate committee to scrutinize President Trump's eldest son, arguing the same congressional oversight applied to Hunter Biden should apply to presidential families of both parties. Driving the news: The Monday letter to Senate Judiciary chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and ranking member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) asks for an investigation into "private financial benefit, preferential treatment, or access" tied to presidential family relationships. Curtis wants the committee to subpoena both sons to testify about "any instances in which their relationship to the President was invoked or understood to provide value." Catch up quick: ProPublica reported that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars toward Trump Jr.'s three-day wedding celebration in the Bahamas, including buying a private-island rental. Curtis also cited Trump Jr.'s ties to prediction markets. Trump Jr. is a paid strategic adviser to Kalshi and sits on Polymarket's advisory board. 1789 Capital, where Trump Jr. is a partner, has invested in Polymarket. Curtis also pointed to Trump family-backed cryptocurrency ventures, international real estate deals involving meetings with foreign heads of state, and Trump Jr.'s reported defense-sector investments. What he's saying: "A toaster is a wedding gift," Curtis wrote on X. "A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else. Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden's foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now. 'Trust us' was not enough then, and it is not enough now." For the record: The White House, Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden have not yet responded to requests for comment. Hunter Biden has denied involving his…

33e1d7779a:e4df3010c5c1e44d.title: "The last invention that man need ever make": The risk of self-improving AI
33e1d7779a:e4df3010c5c1e44d.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:e4df3010c5c1e44d.summary: Of the various ways experts fear AI could kill us all , one is slowly moving closer to reality: AI learning to make itself unstoppable. Why it matters: Recursive Self Improvement, the ability of an AI model to build better versions of itself without human guidance, could make increasingly capable systems harder for humans to control. The RSI threshold doesn't represent danger by itself, but a lack of human control combined with rogue AI agents is a scenario that safety-conscious AI researchers have long feared. Driving the news : Researchers at Anthropic and OpenAI say the process of training new models has grown more automated, coming close to the RSI rubicon. An OpenAI employee told The Information the company has largely automated training new experimental models, with AI systems running experiments as directed by humans and correcting much of their work. Last week, Anthropic shared that its AI training is becoming more automated, with AI leading about 26% of Anthropic's R&D work. AI collaborates on 90% of work, the company says. "AI systems are getting more powerful, and they're increasingly being used to build the next version of themselves," the company said. Reality check: Critics say the milestone is more a function of coding automation than a marker of impending doom or inevitable AI superpowers. While there's been an uptick in troubling AI security incidents in which models outstripped human control, some industry figures see those episodes as evidence of poor internal controls by OpenAI and other companies. Further evidence of that view emerged this week, when The Wall Street Journal reported that independent security researchers used Anthropic's Claude to break into OpenAI in July. Where does RSI come from? Flashback: The concept behind RSI emerged in the 1950s as artificial intelligence became an area of study. British mathematician and statistician Irving John Good described the idea in a 1965 paper : "Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the…

33e1d7779a:b812232a81b4a1a1.title: With $7 trillion on the line, AI safety may always take a backseat to market domination
33e1d7779a:b812232a81b4a1a1.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:b812232a81b4a1a1.summary: The race for AI supremacy between labs, companies and countries may be impossible to reconcile with the push for AI safety, industry insiders tell Axios. Why it matters: The top AI companies are proposing more independent oversight as they seek to engineer an AI slowdown . But trillions of dollars in incentives to keep pushing the frontier — and the money required for such scaling — will always loom larger, critics say. State of play: As AI CEOs pitch the public on self-policing mechanisms and the use of third-party evaluators to make sure their models behave, those same models are sharing less about how they respond to questions and come up with solutions to problems. The sheer complexity of AI systems, as well as the deployment of thousands of somewhat autonomous agents for a variety of tasks, will make real-time auditing or reviewing extremely difficult. There is a trust gap for independent safety groups due to concerns about close ties between the industry and some evaluators, as well as a shared pool of investors and funders in the AI research community. Follow the money: The incentive for speed is a lot more lucrative than the push to slow down in favor of safety. OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing to go public at multi-trillion-dollar valuations, and the companies face pressure to offer incrementally better and better models to justify those valuations. More than $7 trillion will be spent scaling AI over the next five years, per Goldman Sachs. Frontier labs will have to generate a profit on that investment, which means outpacing competitors. That includes keeping customers from pivoting to open-weight model providers, which can be cheaper to run and are viewed by some as a safer alternative. Between the lines: AI is getting harder for anyone to monitor, making it unclear how the seemingly conflicted priorities of safety and rapid-fire model improvement can coexist. Daniel Kokotajlo, former OpenAI researcher and executive director of the AI Futures Project,…

33e1d7779a:06894867de8c97c5.title: U.S.-China "red telephone" could bring a Cold War guardrail to AI
33e1d7779a:06894867de8c97c5.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:06894867de8c97c5.summary: A distinctly Cold War calculus is looming over this week's Trump-Xi summit in Washington, as the U.S. and China weigh an emergency "red phone" for the day AI goes haywire. Why it matters: U.S.-China relations are so brittle that an AI hotline — not a trade pact, strategic slowdown or diplomatic reset — could emerge as the summit's most meaningful outcome. State of play: President Trump has spent the past week lashing out at AI "doomers" and boiling the race down to a single imperative: beat China. Trump has called AI-catastrophe fears a "HOAX" and vowed the U.S. would "not in any way hinder or stifle" AI as it fights to preserve its lead over Beijing. America's leading AI labs largely share Trump's urgency about China, but not his conclusion: many argue the intensity of the race is precisely why global safeguards are needed. The other side: China is every bit as determined to win the AI race, but its leader Xi Jinping — who lands in Washington Wednesday for his first state visit since 2015 — is balancing two competing fears: Falling behind: Xi has no interest in a safety regime that freezes the race with America still ahead. Beijing is pushing cheap, capable open-source models around the world while portraying U.S. chip controls and calls for restraint as a calculated effort to keep China down. Losing control: Xi wants AI powerful enough to transform China's economy, but never so powerful that it slips beyond the control of the Communist Party. Beijing focuses less on Silicon Valley-style extinction scenarios than on nearer-term dangers, like cyberattacks , malicious use and disruptions to critical infrastructure. Zoom in: That narrow overlap is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pitched Chinese officials this weekend on a "notification mechanism" for AI incidents with national-security implications. The Cold War precedent is the hotline Washington and Moscow established after the Cuban Missile Crisis — a direct channel designed to keep accidents and ambiguity…

33e1d7779a:787f03ab7790e57b.title: GOP's war for eyeballs
33e1d7779a:787f03ab7790e57b.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:787f03ab7790e57b.summary: Republicans are starting to trounce Democrats in political spending across the Senate map, and that advantage is now showing up in one of the metrics campaigns care about most: impressions. Why it matters: Money matters in a campaign's closing weeks, but what campaigns are ultimately buying is voters' attention — and the price varies, depending on who is buying and when they place their ads. Beginning in September, campaigns and super PACs start competing for the same finite supply of advertising inventory. But the campaigns are guaranteed lower rates. Republicans are generating substantially more impressions — an estimate of the number of times an ad is seen — but their advantage isn't nearly as large as the spending disparity would suggest. The intrigue: North Carolina is the only key battleground where Republicans have been spending more for fewer impressions in the first weeks of September. Democrats generated 245 million impressions supporting former Gov. Roy Cooper, compared with 226 million for Republican Michael Whatley— even while being outspent by Republicans $10.6 million to $9 million. Whatley has been consistently trailing Cooper in the polls. It is forcing Republicans to weigh whether to begin pulling resources there. One key GOP super PAC took down $6.5 million worth of ads for October, as Semafor first reported . By the numbers: From Sept. 1 through Sept. 17, Republican advertisers generated 502 million impressions in Texas, compared with 331 million for Democrats, according to data compiled by Kinetiq Political Insights. Republicans, relying heavily on super PACs to bolster Attorney General Ken Paxton , spent $37 million over that period. Democrats spent $9.5 million, with much of that coming directly from state Rep. James Talarico's campaign. In Ohio: Republican ads generated 406 million impressions supporting Sen. Jon Husted, compared with 320 million for former Sen. Sherrod Brown. Outside GOP groups accounted for much of Husted's advertising,…

33e1d7779a:fa2ce44f827a1f51.title: Trump and Mamdani's unlikely rapport endures in New York
33e1d7779a:fa2ce44f827a1f51.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:fa2ce44f827a1f51.summary: President Trump and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani struck a warm tone Monday during their third in-person meeting and agreed to deepen talks over a major housing project in Queens. Why it matters: The friendly encounter showed Trump and Mamdani's unusual personal rapport has endured despite their recent political clashes — and fresh disagreements on display Monday. Driving the news: During their meeting, Trump and Mamdani agreed to step up talks over the mayor's plan to build 12,000 affordable homes on a deck over the sprawling Sunnyside Yard in Queens, the two said during a briefing after the talks. "They've been talking about developing that for 50 years. So maybe they have a shot at doing it," said Trump, who met with Mamdani ahead of the UN General Assembly . Zoom in: Their differences were also on display: Mamdani said all members of the press should be allowed White House access, moments before Trump defended his decision to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Mamdani said he discussed his "very strong opinions about how we can keep New Yorkers safe, how we can keep immigrant New Yorkers safe" with Trump during the meeting. Still, Trump said he wanted Mamdani "to be a great mayor" and that he "certainly" has "great potential." Context: Trump and Mamdani's first two White House meetings were unexpectedly cordial , and the two have kept in touch by text , Axios has reported. Zoom out: Their policy differences have persisted, with tensions resurfacing recently over immigration and taxes. New York City led a coalition of cities and counties in a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration's new "public charge" immigration rule. Trump has attacked the mayor's tax on luxury properties owned by nonresidents.

33e1d7779a:b610071ac1211030.title: "People are pissed off": House Dems sneer as one of their own backs a Republican
33e1d7779a:b610071ac1211030.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:b610071ac1211030.summary: Rep. Jared Golden 's decision to endorse one of House Republicans' most vulnerable incumbents is going down like a lead balloon among his fellow House Democrats. Why it matters: The anger won't have much impact on Golden (D-Maine), who is retiring, but it could blow back on his closest ally, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.). "People are pissed off," a House Democrat speaking on the condition of anonymity to share details of private discussions told Axios, adding, "He is doing Gluesenkamp Perez no favors ... this will hurt her." The Washington Democrat, who often breaks from party leadership and moves as a unit with Golden, "is going to have to figure out how she navigates around the suspicion this will create for her next Congress," this lawmaker said. "He is leaving," said a senior House Democrat. "Marie is a bigger problem." Driving the news: Golden wrote an op-ed in a local newspaper in Rep. Mike Lawler's New York district endorsing the Republican for reelection. Golden cited his work with Lawler on several pieces of legislation, most notably their bill to exempt lobstermen from certain federal environmental regulations. "Mike Lawler has been a true partner to me and a friend to fishing families he will never represent," Golden wrote. "I strongly back him, and I hope voters send him back to work." Between the lines: The endorsement comes after Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, who previously co-chaired the centrist Blue Dog Coalition, repeatedly broke with party leadership on key procedural votes in recent weeks. Twice this month, the two Democrats provided Republican leadership with the votes needed to advance their legislation to the floor, including bills strongly opposed by Democratic leaders. The repeated defections have sparked enormous anger within the House Democratic caucus, with some lawmakers calling to punish Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez. What they're saying: Democrats met Golden's endorsement with contemptuous dismissal, arguing that it will do…

33e1d7779a:16c03c4b01730e7a.title: Ariz. activists build map to show federal agents at polls
33e1d7779a:16c03c4b01730e7a.author: Brittany Gibson
33e1d7779a:16c03c4b01730e7a.summary: Arizona immigration advocates are building an interactive map to alert people if federal agents are spotted near polling places this fall. Why it matters: It's illegal for federal law enforcement officers to interfere with the right to vote, but for months Republicans in D.C. and in Arizona's state house have floated the idea of ICE agents or National Guard troops being deployed to voting precincts. When asked in May whether he was considering sending ICE or Guard troops to polling places, President Trump said he'd "do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections." That raised concerns across the country about potential voter intimidation — particularly in places such as Arizona that have large immigrant populations . The big picture: The online heat map of ICE activity that's being developed in Arizona will show live updates of polling places where ICE agents are spotted, along with past enforcement activity in Maricopa and Pima counties, the state's two most populous counties. There's been a noticeable increase in ICE activity in these counties recently, said Karime Rodriguez, a spokesperson for the Arizona Center for Empowerment (ACE), a social justice-oriented nonprofit that works with immigrants that is behind the heat map. "Just the simple threat of ICE presence is enough to keep somebody from voting," Rodriguez said. "It's all a coordinated effort to keep people away from voting and to make voting more confusing and less accessible." She added the threat could be particularly acute for people coming from mixed-status households, where someone they live with isn't voting but isn't a citizen. Catch up quick: Arizona's Republican-led state Senate considered a bill that would have required ICE agents at the polls this November, but it didn't pass. State Sen. Jake Hoffman (R) argued such a requirement would make elections safer, echoing the Trump administration. "When voters see the rules applied fairly and consistently, confidence in the outcome…

33e1d7779a:297886477d539255.title: Trump inaudible during White House TV pool blackout
33e1d7779a:297886477d539255.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:297886477d539255.summary: President Trump was inaudible during a press conference Monday after the TV pool suspended coverage, with White House-provided video without usable audio of his remarks. Why it matters: It's a remarkable and immediate ramification of Trump's attempt to limit pool access. The pool serves hundreds of journalists, so losing independent TV coverage can limit what the media — and the public — can see and hear. Driving the news: President Trump announced a ban on CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Friday, confiscating their credentials on Saturday over what he termed "FAKE NEWS". CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit on Monday seeking to restore their access, arguing the ban violates the First Amendment. The decision to pull pooled TV coverage is a rare display of unified pushback from fiercely competitive networks against the administration's attempt to dictate what the public sees and how. Thought bubble, via Axios' Brittany Gibson, one of the poolers: The White House Press Pool, by design and by necessity, is a collaborative effort amongst the nation's top news outlets. These outlets, Axios included, are daily witnesses to arguably the most powerful office in the world and its revolving occupants. The daily reports of what we're able to see, hear, photograph are carefully and quickly shared for the public record and are part of holding the office accountable to the people. What the pool is How it works: The White House press pool is a rotating group of journalists who stay by the president's side throughout his public appearances and share their reporting, audio and footage with the rest of the media. The pool includes about 20 journalists. They travel with Trump on Air Force One and cram into the Oval Office, providing updates. The TV coverage relies on five networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC — that take turns providing live footage. What the pool does The big picture: Trump is constantly on the move, so the pool makes it easier and less expensive to document…

33e1d7779a:0c9314bee4cc327b.title: "National security" becomes Trump's executive sledgehammer
33e1d7779a:0c9314bee4cc327b.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:0c9314bee4cc327b.summary: What do a White House ban on journalists, a 250-foot arch near the nation's capital and Greenland have in common? President Trump needs all of them for national security purposes, he and his administration have argued. Why it matters: As he's unilaterally shattered presidential norms, Trump has justified his sweeping policy priorities with a familiar two-word rationale: national security. Driving the news: On the morning that the three banned outlets (CNN, MS NOW and Politico) sued the administration , Trump claimed that "FAKE NEWS" is "a threat to our National Security." It's not the first time the administration has said its press restrictions were a national security must: That was also part of the reasoning for new rules for Pentagon reporters , a war on leakers and subpoenas of journalists. National security purposes are a broad bucket that the president has also used to justify his D.C. redesign: Trump pitched his proposed " triumphal arch " as a dual-use facility housing snipers, drones and ammunition storage "for National Security purposes." That's also why the president was adamant his White House ballroom project must proceed (after he demolished the East Wing). The White House declined to comment beyond the president's post. Zoom out: The national security rationale has also fueled the administration's deregulatory AI approach. Earlier this month, Justice Department attorneys argued that laws that get in the way of a growing AI industry "threaten national security" in a statement of interest backing AI companies in The New York Times' copyright infringement lawsuit. What they're saying: The executive's use of national security as a justification for policy can trigger "extreme deference" in the courts, says Kimberly Wehle, a University of Baltimore law professor. Wehle notes the expanded executive power seen in Trump 2.0 has its origins in the Bush-era advancement of the unitary executive theory — though the national psyche today does not necessarily…

33e1d7779a:452d6a56fc54e3f7.title: Ahead of Sam Altman's UN address, OpenAI proposes new ways to track AI misalignment risks
33e1d7779a:452d6a56fc54e3f7.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:452d6a56fc54e3f7.summary: OpenAI on Monday released international AI safety standards as world leaders, namely the U.S. and China, weigh how to mitigate risk. Why it matters: The U.S. approach to coordinating on AI risk with China will be heavily informed by industry recommendations. Driving the news: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng over the weekend discussed a U.S.-China AI dialogue to notify the other country when AI incidents reached national security risk levels. The devil is in the details and OpenAI is proposing solutions that CEO Sam Altman will cover in his address at the United Nations Security Council in New York on Wednesday. What they're saying: OpenAI recommends leveraging AI safety institutes around the world to facilitate standard-setting through the U.S. Center for AI Security and Innovation, which is part of the Commerce Department. The company also recommends shared global measurements for classifying incidents and how to track, report and respond to alignment issues. The goal is to have international standards for incidents that happen before deployment in test settings and those that occur in the real world, an OpenAI official told Axios. What we're watching: Expect AI labs to continue chiming in as all eyes are on President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping's meetings and a state dinner featuring industry heavy hitters later this week.

33e1d7779a:e6c5d419ee4c3f84.title: Exclusive: How Sen. Schatz is talking about climate in an affordability crisis
33e1d7779a:e6c5d419ee4c3f84.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:e6c5d419ee4c3f84.summary: Americans are "connecting the dots" between climate and affordability strain, Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) said Monday at an Axios House event on the sidelines of Climate Week and the UN General Assembly. Why it matters: But as pocketbook issues dominate a critical midterm race, Schatz says that doesn't mean the first thing he mentions to constituents is climate. Still, climate-tangent conversations — like utility prices and the data center boom — are looming over the polls. Driving the news: "I think we should talk about climate in the context of people not being able to afford their lives," Schatz told Axios' Ben Geman, pointing to insurance non-renewals, soaring gas prices and rising utility bills . "It's not that difficult anymore for us to be able to say, look, one of the reasons things are getting more expensive is we're not addressing the climate crisis," he said, criticizing the federal government's renewables roadblocks. "The climate imperatives used to have to be balanced against people's pocketbooks, and now they are perfectly lined up," he added. "We do not have to make trade-offs. They are deciding to make the planet worse and make your pocketbook situation worse." Catch up quick: Schatz has been a leading congressional voice on climate issues, representing a heavily petroleum -dependent U.S. state with high energy prices that's at particular risk from the impacts of climate change. The state has taken on an ambitious clean energy initiative that aims for 100% renewable energy by 2035 on the neighbor islands, including Maui and Hawaiʻi. Friction point: The sweeping GOP budget bill signed into law by President Trump last year phased out wind, solar, and electric vehicle subsidies that the prior administration championed as tools to bolster clean tech. It's one front in Trump's broader rollback of Biden-era climate policies , including moves to kill regulations and a slowdown in permitting of renewables projects. In particular, administration officials…

33e1d7779a:d7dd7d74f5b6d588.title: For the first time, Merz's CDU is out of a German state parliament after AfD won.
33e1d7779a:d7dd7d74f5b6d588.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:d7dd7d74f5b6d588.summary: Germany's ruling center-right party, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union, was shut out of a state parliament for the first time Sunday as the far-right Alternative for Germany scored its second victory this month. Why it matters: The result marks the third state election AfD has won — and its second this month — underscoring its growing strength even as Germany's other major parties refuse to govern with it. Driving the news: Merz, who has low approval ratings, told reporters that "reforms have to come." AfD won about 38% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the CDU recorded its worst result in any German state election since World War II. The CDU fell from 13% to 4.9% and lost all representation. In Berlin's state election, the Left more than doubled its vote share to 25.7% and finished first for the first time. Flashback: AfD won its first state election in Thuringia in 2024, though other parties kept it out of government because they refused to enter into a coalition. Earlier this month, it won 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt, but fell just three seats short of a majority. It is now seeking enough outside support to form Germany's first far-right state government since World War II. Vice President JD Vance met with AfD's co-leader days before last year's federal election and told the Munich Security Conference there was "no room for firewalls," referring to mainstream parties' refusal to govern with the AfD. The big picture: Germany's political firewall against AfD is rooted partly in the country's post-World War II consensus against returning the far-right to government and has been reinforced by intelligence concerns about extremism within the party. Germany's domestic intelligence service continues to monitor AfD nationally as a suspected extremist organization. A court in February blocked the agency from classifying the entire party as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization while a broader case proceeds. The anti-migration…

33e1d7779a:f380e8940e59181a.title: Trump weighed strikes against Houthis in Yemen before holding off
33e1d7779a:f380e8940e59181a.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:f380e8940e59181a.summary: President Trump over the weekend considered ordering a strike against the Houthis in Yemen before deciding to hold off for now, two U.S. officials said. Why it matters: Trump was caught between wanting to help his friend and ally, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and avoiding getting entangled on a new front in the Middle East. Catch up quick: Ten days ago, bin Salman (MBS) called Trump twice on the same day, urging him to launch strikes against the Houthis as the Iran-backed group closed in on a vital Red Sea chokepoint. Trump rejected the request and agreed only to help the Saudis with intelligence and targeting data. U.S. officials said at the time they wouldn't take military action as long as the Houthis did not interrupt non-Saudi ship traffic in the Red Sea. Several days later, U.S. diplomats met with Houthi officials and received assurances that the rebel group has no intention of closing the Bab-al-Mandeb Strait. Behind the scenes: But late last week the Saudis, who were having trouble pushing back on Houthi advances, again asked Trump to take military action in Yemen, the two U.S. officials said. They said that over the weekend Trump held consultations with his senior advisers about the possibility of strikes against the Houthis. One U.S. official said the commander of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), Adm. Brad Cooper, prepared options for airstrikes in Yemen and presented them to Secretary of Defense Hegseth on Saturday. But Trump ultimately decided to hold off, another U.S. official said. The New York Times first reported about Trump's deliberations around the possible strike in Yemen. The White House and the Saudi embassy in Washington declined to comment. What they're saying: "The president changed his mind and did not want to open a Pandora's box by striking because it could cause the Houthis to hold the Bab-al-Mandeb at risk and create a second choke point," Alex Plitsas, a fellow at the Atlantic Council and former Pentagon official, told…

33e1d7779a:9c30e7d1eb8c8f9b.title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico to sue White House over blocked access
33e1d7779a:9c30e7d1eb8c8f9b.author: Sara Fischer
33e1d7779a:9c30e7d1eb8c8f9b.summary: CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Monday said they plan to file a First Amendment lawsuit against the White House, arguing the president and the administration violated their rights by blocking their access over the weekend. Why it matters : Many presidents have had a contentious relationship with certain outlets, but none have gone so far as to unilaterally block them. Zoom in : "This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the three news organizations said in a joint statement on Monday. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting," they said. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." Zoom out : The lawsuit is a historic show of solidarity amongst the banned outlets, as they and other newsrooms continue to face unprecedented pressure from The Trump administration. Figures within the administration have argued the president has the right to ban reporters from certain spaces, but legal experts argue precedent overwhelmingly backs the news outlets. This is a breaking news story.

33e1d7779a:9475e64bd8338199.title: Exclusive: Beshear says next president must go big on housing
33e1d7779a:9475e64bd8338199.author: Holly Otterbein
33e1d7779a:9475e64bd8338199.summary: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear signaled in an interview with Axios that he would put America's housing affordability crisis at the center of his campaign if he ran for president in 2028. Why it matters: It's the latest sign that Beshear, who just kicked off a national book tour, is moving closer to a bid for the White House. Driving the news: Beshear said the next president should pursue a massive housing initiative — with strict guidelines to ensure the money is spent quickly. "There's a chance for the next presidential administration or the next Congress to make a big, bold investment in housing that could have us building millions of units all over the United States," he said. "We cannot do this in drips and drabs. It can't be mild investments over a period of time." Echoing the "Abundance" movement, which calls for slashing regulations in order to lower housing costs, Beshear said federal dollars sent to states should be used quickly or withdrawn. "If you tie the federal dollars to that timing, you will break through the regulation and the NIMBYism," he said. Beshear declined to put a specific price tag on his vision, saying that those details could be discussed with lawmakers. But he said $150 billion in federal spending could theoretically lead to $1 trillion of housing being built if enough outside financing were leveraged. By the numbers: Escalating home prices have become a major political issue in recent years. Sixty-four percent of American adults say they're "very concerned" about the cost of housing, according to a Pew Research Center poll in July. The intrigue: After talking policy, we asked Beshear about rumors swirling in Democratic circles that he could announce a run for president as soon as December. "I would tell you that that is solely a rumor," he said of the winter timeline. "I haven't made any final decisions yet." But, sounding as if he's close to making up his mind, Beshear added, "Listen, I don't want to leave a broken country to my kids."

33e1d7779a:7096bacd140fcda4.title: Many ex-aides to Harris betting against a 2028 run
33e1d7779a:7096bacd140fcda4.author: Holly Otterbein
33e1d7779a:7096bacd140fcda4.summary: Many of those who know Kamala Harris best think she ultimately won't run for the White House in 2028. Why it matters: What the former vice president decides to do is one of the biggest X factors in the next presidential contest: Early polls suggest Harris is the frontrunner to be the Democratic nominee, and if she opted out, it would scramble the primary. Zoom in: Over the past year, a surprisingly large number of former aides, surrogates and donors to Harris have told Axios they believe she won't launch another campaign. They argue that the moves she's making — hitting the trail for midterm candidates, going on the podcast circuit, and writing a book — might make her look like a contender-in-waiting, but actually amount to her simply trying to maintain influence. Harris has said publicly and privately she hasn't made up her mind yet, and some of her former aides concede they could be wrong — or could even be "wishcasting" because they don't want her to pursue another bid. This week, we surveyed eight former Harris aides and advisers, including those who worked for her at a senior level, to get their most up-to-date read. Only one thought Harris probably will run. Two said it's a coin-flip, and five said she likely won't. Here's why: She's doing "the bare minimum" to stay in the 2028 conversation, as one past aide put it. Harris' former staffers argue that if she were gung-ho about running she'd be hiring more, traveling more, and inserting herself into policy debates more often. She's a rational actor. Former aides say Harris is well aware of the hurdles that would await her if she ran again. "She's a realist and an astute political observer, and she knows her candidacy could get bogged down in a 2024 rearview mirror," said a second former aide. The money might not be there. Many high-dollar donors are still furious about Harris' loss and don't want her to run again. Top Democratic donor Reid Hoffman said last week that she'd face "a very challenging path" in…

33e1d7779a:97295b9a43dc5d0e.title: Trump to meet with Zelensky as Russia-Ukraine attacks intensify
33e1d7779a:97295b9a43dc5d0e.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:97295b9a43dc5d0e.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said after a phone call with President Trump on Sunday that the two will meet this week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Why it matters: The meeting comes as the White House works to broker an agreement between Russia and Ukraine to take reciprocal steps to deescalate and resume negotiations — and as fighting between the two sides has intensified in recent days. Zelensky's chief negotiator and the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, Rustem Umerov, told Axios he's been working with White House envoys in recent days to organize the meeting, which is expected to happen Tuesday. Driving the news: The meeting will take place several days after Trump signed a Russia sanctions bill and approved the biggest arms deal between the U.S. and Ukraine since assuming office — two steps Ukraine has been pushing for months. What he's saying: "An important conversation, and we got through a lot. We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum," Zelensky wrote on X. Zelensky said Ukraine is ready "to take really serious steps" to reach a deescalation deal with Russia. Behind the scenes: A source familiar with the call said Trump repeatedly asked Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. The strikes are driving up global diesel prices. "The word diesel came up many times during the call," the source said. The intrigue: Earlier this week the Kyiv Independent reported that the Ukrainian government was "growing increasingly frustrated" with White House envoy Steve Witkoff. The story came out several days after Witkoff and Trump adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time since the war began. Umerov told Axios the story was false. "I believe that the work of American negotiators should be assessed by people who are directly involved in the negotiation process and work closely with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner," he said. He added…

33e1d7779a:f446c5a196324365.title: Three Republican power players walk into a D.C. bar, and ...
33e1d7779a:f446c5a196324365.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:f446c5a196324365.summary: It sounds like the start of an only-in-D.C. joke: Three Republican power players walk into a bar for a freewheeling conversation. They unwittingly sit next to a liberal comic. She then skewers them in an Instagram post recounting their chat. Why it matters: It became no laughing matter for one of the Republicans —oilman Harry Sargeant — who's trying to improve his uneasy relations with the Trump administration, partly related to his business dealings in Venezuela. His rapprochement efforts were complicated last month when senior administration officials became aware of the comic's social media post, in which she alleged that Sargeant spoke negatively about President Trump. The big picture: The story illustrates the panopticon of modern society and, especially, the nation's capital. Everyone is watched and being watched. And the White House takes notes on who's naughty and nice to Trump. Zoom in: The episode unfolded Aug. 18 in the Bourbon Lounge of the Four Seasons hotel in D.C., where comic Suzanne Lambert was working on jokes for an upcoming set, she said in a post to her 495,000 Instagram followers that had 2 million views before she took it down. In the video, Lambert said she coincidentally wound up sitting next to Sargeant and noted a vibe shift when two other men walked in: Pete Marocco and Gentry Beach. Marocco was described by Fox News as the "mastermind" who helped dismantle USAID early in the second Trump administration. Politico subsequently reported he had tensions with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Beach was the subject of a Wall Street Journal profile last year about how the lobbyist name-drops his longtime friend and presidential son Donald Trump Jr., in international business affairs, including one involving a Russian oil deal. Inside the room: Lambert said her in post that she was just "minding my business" but started to pay more attention when the men at the bar began "spouting off about Trump. I hear Trump, Trump, Trump, Trump." At one…

33e1d7779a:c7e23f07c6a70c5a.title: The tech battle to build your AI assistant
33e1d7779a:c7e23f07c6a70c5a.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:c7e23f07c6a70c5a.summary: The long-promised personal AI assistant is finally arriving, with a suddenly crowded field of agents offering to run pieces of your everyday life. Why it matters: For years, tech's "personal assistants" were little more than voice-controlled search boxes. Rapid advances in AI are finally giving them the memory, judgment and autonomy to act on our behalf. Catch up fast: Chatbots answer questions. AI agents can actually do things — shopping, making calls, booking tickets, managing calendars and navigating the web. The model first took off in coding and other professional work. Now it's spilling into the far more intimate terrain of everyday life. The intrigue: OpenAI is expected to enter the market soon after hiring the creator of OpenClaw — a breakout hit among AI power users earlier this year — to "drive the next generation of personal agents." Driving the news: A consumer-agent race has erupted almost overnight, with startups and tech giants pursuing the same basic idea — persistent digital proxies that know your life. Instinct has become buzzy by connecting to users' email, messages, screen, audio and location — then proactively texting or calling to help run their lives. It recently added its own email addresses and the ability to make phone calls, and is now in talks for a $10 billion valuation . Grok Bot, launched by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI in August, gives persistent agents their own cloud computers, lets them sign into users' apps and keeps them working around the clock. Meta's Muse brought the concept to a broader consumer audience this month with a polished app, a customizable avatar and deep integration with Meta's ecosystem. Apple's Siri is finally getting its AI overhaul , bringing more context and capability to an assistant already built into hundreds of millions of devices. The big picture: The battle to become your personal agent is also a battle to become the keeper of your personal information and data. The frontier AI race has revolved around raw…

33e1d7779a:df64b9064d30c1a1.title: Trump's proposed Washington arch to become sniper, drone facility
33e1d7779a:df64b9064d30c1a1.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:df64b9064d30c1a1.summary: President Trump said Sunday morning his proposed " triumphal arch " in Washington will become a dual-use facility housing snipers, drones and ammunition storage. Why it matters: The president is now framing construction of the arch as a national security issue — much like he did with the East Wing ballroom /military complex at the White House. What they're saying: "At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch, planned since the Civil War Era many years ago, at the Receptive Circle adjoining the Arlington Memorial Bridge, into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage," Trump posted on Truth Social. Catch up quick: The proposed 250-foot arch would be one of the largest such monuments in the world, sparking concerns that it could interfere with other national symbols, block views and even complicate landings for pilots at nearby airports. The New York Times reported this week that the National Park Service is rushing through a final review of the project ahead of a likely approval in November. The NPS's own August report indicated the construction of the arch would have adverse effects on many nearby monuments and landmarks. This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

33e1d7779a:809cbe0004e4337b.title: How Trump 2.0's stock market stacks up with predecessors
33e1d7779a:809cbe0004e4337b.author: Dan Primack
33e1d7779a:809cbe0004e4337b.summary: Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals The stock market soared during the first 20 months of President Trump's second term, but slightly underperformed the same period of his first term. Why it matters: Trump considers the stock market to be a proxy for the economy, even though many economists disagree. By the numbers: The S&P 500 rose nearly 27.6% between inauguration day and this past Friday's close, compared to 28.5% during his first term. The gap at 20 months is closer than it was at the one-year mark , with Trump 2.0 leapfrogging former President Biden but still trailing former President Obama. Zoom in: Trump 2.0 also trails Trump 1.0 in terms of Dow Jones Industrial Average and Nasdaq Composite performance, but is ahead on the Russell 3000. Dow Jones Industrial Avg Trump 2.0: 18.8% Biden: 0.3% Trump 1.0: 33.8% Obama : 28.1% Nasdaq Composite Trump 2.0: 35.1% Biden: (-12.6%) Trump 1.0: 43.5% Obama: 51.4%

33e1d7779a:a95bd4419a187bb5.title: Trump wants a new AI czar and an "AI Force" modeled on Space Force
33e1d7779a:a95bd4419a187bb5.author: Andrew Pantazi
33e1d7779a:a95bd4419a187bb5.summary: President Trump announced Saturday he is creating an "AI Force" modeled on the Space Force and will soon name a new AI czar, doubling down on his push to accelerate artificial intelligence development with limited regulation. Why it matters: The White House isn't backing down from its laissez-faire approach to AI, even as the industry's biggest leaders call for stronger safety rules and as public concern about AI intensifies. The latest: Trump offered few details on what this AI Force would actually do, what budget it would have or where it would be placed in the federal government. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. His Truth Social post said the government would "not in any way hinder or stifle" AI's growth but would look for "BAD" behavior using "our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System." Catch up quick: Trump has hardened his anti-regulation position during an extraordinary month of warnings from inside the AI industry. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis — the Nobel laureate who co-founded and chairs Google DeepMind — have all called for slowing AI development as their systems become more powerful. The intrigue: The AI czar position would revive a role that the White House didn't plan to fill six months ago. David Sacks left the formal AI and crypto czar job in March, though he remains influential as co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:062e32e6ad36fc6a.title: Iran war causes global pain at the pump
33e1d7779a:062e32e6ad36fc6a.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:062e32e6ad36fc6a.summary: Data: Axios research. Note: Some countries use a quota system for gasoline. Malaysia's figure reflects the unsubsidized market rate. Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios The Iran war is driving fuel prices higher worldwide, leading to angry protests around the globe and straining the economies of countries that have nothing to do with the war. Why it matters: It's not just driving up prices in the U.S. The war is causing problems around the world — in some cases far worse than anything Americans are experiencing. The surge in prices squeezes consumers, and worsens the finances of governments trying to contain the shock — especially poorer and developing countries with little fiscal running room. It affects many nations that are also facing higher prices for natural gas, diesel and other fuels. Zoom out: The map above, based on World Bank data, shows the upward global trend. Yes, but: Price increases vary greatly from country to country. A number of countries that are heavily reliant on fuel imports, like Pakistan and Myanmar, have seen steep price hikes. But the U.S., the world's largest oil and gasoline producer, also has soaring prices. Crude oil prices, the biggest input into gasoline costs, are set on global markets. The U.S. federal government, unlike some nations, has not set caps or subsidies on retail prices. Context: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries are also helping to boost motor fuel prices, especially diesel. The big picture: With no resolution to the conflict in sight, many governments face hard choices — strain their budgets with fuel support or face the political consequences of higher fuel costs. State of play: Dozens of nations have taken steps to cap, subsidize or lower taxes on various fuels, per the International Energy Agency. Governments are also taking steps to reduce demand, such as more remote work and limiting government travel. The International Monetary Fund is worried about the fiscal hit from price supports, especially if they…

33e1d7779a:0a3cca8e1bf8d320.title: Football drives GOP's TV ad blitz for the midterms
33e1d7779a:0a3cca8e1bf8d320.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:0a3cca8e1bf8d320.summary: Republicans scrambling for midterm momentum are making a massive bet on football, pouring millions into advertising during the country's biggest NFL and college games. Why it matters: Across the country, Republicans are trying to hold onto male voters — football's core audience and a critical part of President Trump's 2024 coalition. After winning 55% of the male vote in 2024, Trump has seen his standing with men deteriorate. A new Fox News poll puts his approval among them at 42%, down 9 points from a year ago. The signs of slippage are particularly clear among young men. A spring Harvard Youth Poll found men ages 18–29 favored a Democratic congressional candidate by 8 points, after reporting an even split between Trump and Harris in 2024. By the numbers: Part of Republicans' plan to try to change the midterm vibe is to capitalize on their financial advantage by dominating the football airwaves. They ran 5,546 TV spots during the NFL and college games and pre-and-postgame programming where they advertised most heavily last weekend, compared with 471 for Democrats — nearly 12 times as many, according to ad-tracking data obtained by Axios. Republicans' biggest presence was during the blockbuster Texas-Ohio State matchup, which featured teams from two states with competitive Senate races. The pro-GOP Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) super PAC spent $2 million, airing ads in every quarter before 14 million viewers on ABC. The national coverage meant viewers nationwide saw Senate ads that were targeted to Texas or Ohio. Zoom in: Nowhere is the GOP's football strategy more apparent than in Michigan, where the Senate race could determine control of that chamber. SLF struck a deal with a vendor that manages sports programming in Michigan bars, putting its ads on more than 1,000 TVs at 150 bars across the state. Republicans launched the effort after Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed made critical remarks about football, which became the focus of the ads. A…

33e1d7779a:1d48f56297c3af3f.title: Google is the latest AI lab with a security testing mishap
33e1d7779a:1d48f56297c3af3f.author: Sam Sabin
33e1d7779a:1d48f56297c3af3f.summary: Google's Gemini AI model broke into three companies' systems using basic hacking techniques during model testing earlier this year. Why it matters: Google was one of the only AI labs that hadn't yet publicly disclosed a security breach involving their agents during routine pre-deployment testing. Driving the news: Google confirmed the three incidents, which happened in May, on Friday. The incidents happened as part of a test run that third-party evaluator Irregular was operating — similar to other security breaches involving OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta's AI models. The Wall Street Journal first reported the incidents. What they're saying : "Safe development of powerful AI models is critical and we invest deeply in this area," Heather Adkins, vice president of security engineering at Google, said in a statement. Adkins added that her team contacted the affected entities and "worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes." An Irregular spokesperson confirmed to Axios that the Gemini incident involved the same security issues that also led to similar incidents involving other AI labs' models. The spokesperson also said in a statement all "relevant labs were notified in late July" and that "all known issues on our end were remedied and resolved weeks ago." Zoom in: The hacks happened while Gemini was completing a "capture the flag" hacking exercise, where the model was asked to retrieve information from software operated by a fictional company inside a testing environment, per the WSJ. However, the fictional company had the same name as a real one. In one case, the model guessed passwords for a protected system until it gained access. In the other two cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that then allowed it to access other protected systems. Yes, but: Google's model stopped their actions as soon as they realized they accessed real companies. The intrigue: Irregular told the Wall Street Journal that the…

33e1d7779a:d6604d6d3eca0755.title: DOJ won't enforce handgun ban for 18- to 20-year-olds
33e1d7779a:d6604d6d3eca0755.author: Andrew Pantazi
33e1d7779a:d6604d6d3eca0755.summary: The Justice Department said Friday it will not criminally enforce a 1968 federal law barring licensed gun dealers from selling handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds, after its Office of Legal Counsel concluded the restriction violated the Second Amendment. Why it matters: The Trump administration is telling federal prosecutors not to enforce a law passed by Congress, even though the Supreme Court has never ruled on its constitutionality. The decision could give adults under the age of 21 access to the country's licensed handgun market, though it remains unclear whether dealers will begin selling to them immediately. The latest: The Thursday opinion signed by Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser stands as controlling legal advice for the executive branch, though it isn't a court ruling and doesn't bind judges or erase the law. Gaiser wrote that 18- to 20-year-olds are adults protected by the Second Amendment, and the right to own handguns includes the ability to buy them. While the opinion said criminal enforcement was unconstitutional, it didn't address whether agencies like the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives could continue administrative enforcement of the ban. The White House, the Department of Justice, and ATF have not yet responded to Axios' requests for comment. The other side: Giffords, a gun-safety advocacy group, called the move "illegal and dangerous" and said it would "do everything we can to fight this." Kris Brown, president of Brady: United Against Gun Violence, said the opinion "does not change the law itself" and misreads the nation's history of gun regulation. "The provision prohibiting the sale of handguns to 18-to-20-year-olds has protected public safety for generations," Brown said in a statement. "This opinion by the Department of Justice is yet more evidence that the Trump administration is prioritizing the gun industry's wishlist, rather than protecting American lives." State of play: The Supreme Court has denied…

33e1d7779a:7a7684e6d007b559.title: Trump claims security, military deal with Denmark over Greenland
33e1d7779a:7a7684e6d007b559.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:7a7684e6d007b559.summary: President Trump said late Friday the U.S. has struck a deal with Denmark that will give America "permanent control over security" in Greenland. Why it matters: Control over Greenland has been a fixation of Trump's for years and a wedge in U.S. relations with Europe. Any such deal could potentially reduce tensions with the EU, though it's unclear how residents of the island itself will take to the pact. What they're saying: " I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns," Trump posted on Truth Social. "There will be NO COST to the United States!" The other side: The Associated Press cited the Danish prime minister as saying the three countries will sign the deal in New York next week during the UN General Assembly. Between the lines: Trump said in his post that the U.S. will build a large military presence on the island, though he did not specify where or how large. He also indicated the U.S. would have a veto over other countries having military bases or sensitive investments on the island. Fox News, citing an unnamed U.S. official, said the deal stops short of full sovereignty over Greenland, but is designed to persist even if the island becomes an independent nation someday. Context: Danish and Greenlandic leaders have consistently told Trump that Greenland is not for sale. Under a 1951 defense agreement with Denmark, the U.S. already has military access to the island. But Trump has repeatedly claimed that the U.S. needs Greenland. Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte discussed a Greenland framework in January that briefly abated talk of the U.S. annexing the island. However, Trump's desire to annex new land has come up repeatedly during his second term.

33e1d7779a:5d5fa6e7ac5a35c9.title: USPS made mail slower to cut costs. Midterm ballots will test the system.
33e1d7779a:5d5fa6e7ac5a35c9.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:5d5fa6e7ac5a35c9.summary: The U.S. Postal Service has slowed down mail deliveries so much it's failing to meet even its lowered performance targets, a new report from the Government Accountability Office found. Why it matters: The Postal Service is part of the connective tissue of American life: delivering prescription drugs and ballots , carrying government notices and bills, helping businesses reach customers across the country. Now its attempts to shore up its finances are disproportionately affecting rural communities . The big picture: The Postal Service has given itself more time to deliver some first-class mail, the congressional watchdog's report notes, which millions of Americans rely on for medications, bills, paychecks, financial documents and mail-in ballots. The USPS is expected to fund itself largely through postage and other revenue while also providing universal service to nearly every U.S. address, even where doing so isn't profitable. By the numbers: The USPS added one to two days to expected delivery times for some mail after shifting some transportation from air to ground in 2021. The report said about 24,000 post offices will lose afternoon mail collection if they're more than 50 miles from a regional processing and delivery center, disproportionately affecting rural Americans. The intrigue: The service concerns come just weeks before the midterms, when millions of voters will rely on USPS to return ballots under state-specific deadlines. The Trump administration has pushed to dramatically overhaul the country's mail-in ballot system . What they're saying: "Whenever the post office closes … for rural communities, that takes the heart out of the place," Steve Hutkins, editor of Save the Post Office, tells Axios. "Everybody talks about how slow the mail is now. … The goalposts have moved several times," he said, adding that delivery times have slowed four times since 2010. "It all adds up." "The problem is if you want to cut costs to try to balance the books, you're…

33e1d7779a:462731d4682d78df.title: 2028 Democrats like Newsom and Pritzker lean in on AI safety as Washington stalls
33e1d7779a:462731d4682d78df.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:462731d4682d78df.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a presumptive presidential candidate, is getting louder on AI, releasing an executive order amid the Washington stalemate. Why it matters: Democrats with national profiles this week are seizing on AI alarm, making their positions clear and Newsom – despite some deference shown to other 2028 contender Kamala Harris – wasn't going to sit this one out. Driving the news: Newsom on Friday issued an executive order tackling two major topics of debate inside the beltway this week -- independent auditors and kill switches. He did so taking direct aim at Washington: "With Donald Trump and Congress asleep at the wheel, Governor Gavin Newsom is once again taking the lead to strengthen AI safety for all Americans." Newsom was early to stake out a position on an issue that is increasingly politically salient, signing the first AI executive order in 2023. Between the lines: In the absence of U.S. legislation or more action from the Trump administration, states have stepped in to fill the void on AI regulation, a development some top AI execs sought to avoid. There are more than 600 bills in 47 states about AI, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, up 24% from last year. California, Illinois and Massachusetts are among the states leading the charge. All three are run by Democrats, who are seeking to seize the mantle of AI regulation nationally. Yes, but : Politicians in both parties are using antipathy toward data centers to punish opponents, including GOP candidates in gubernatorial races in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. California has emerged as both the state filling the federal regulatory void and one largely aligned with the frontier AI labs it is regulating. The executive order accelerates the implementation of two bills signed into law last week -- both of which were endorsed by OpenAI and Anthropic -- on independent verification organizations. Newsom's position on a kill switch is also aligned with what frontier labs are…

33e1d7779a:95691fd9f66e6b62.title: Trump bans CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House
33e1d7779a:95691fd9f66e6b62.author: Andrew Pantazi
33e1d7779a:95691fd9f66e6b62.summary: President Trump said Friday he is banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House "effective immediately," escalating his long-running battles with news organizations. Why it matters: Trump is seeking to use White House access against news outlets whose coverage he objects to, while threatening to target additional organizations. Press freedom groups immediately called on news outlets to fight the bans. The latest: Trump's Truth Social post called the three outlets "Fake News" and accused them of reporting "FICTION and LIES," before threatening to also ban other "Fake News Media Outlets." The White House declined to comment beyond Trump's post. CNN, MS NOW, Politico and the White House Correspondents' Association have not responded to Axios' requests for comment. Between the lines: The scope of the ban wasn't immediately clear. As of shortly after the post, CNN continued to work from the White House, the network reported. The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals has previously held that once the White House opens general press facilities to journalists, access can't be denied arbitrarily, and press pass restrictions must come with due process. A divided appellate court last year said the White House does have broader discretion over which journalists enter restricted spaces like the Oval Office and Air Force One. That case, brought by the Associated Press, remains unresolved. Friction point: Trump has previously moved to restrict access for reporters and outlets he has clashed with. In 2018, the White House revoked CNN reporter Jim Acosta's credential. A federal judge later ordered the pass restored. Last year, the administration barred the AP from some events because it continued to use "Gulf of Mexico," sparking the still-pending First Amendment case. State of play: The White House took control of selecting the presidential press pool from the White House Correspondents' Association last year. The Pentagon has also restricted press access, but a federal judge…

33e1d7779a:caf72ea2e33d3a4c.title: GOP's Latino gains fade as deeper gender and generational divides emerge
33e1d7779a:caf72ea2e33d3a4c.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:caf72ea2e33d3a4c.summary: Latino voters swung sharply toward Republicans in 2024. Now, much of that gain is fading as gender and generational divides widen. Why it matters: The GOP breakthrough two years ago hasn't produced a uniformly more conservative Latino electorate, as Democrats have regained ground in polling this year. But an Axios analysis of recent polls shows Latino voters aren't simply swinging right, then left. The data show Latino politics fragmenting from within, as young Latino men and women increasingly split over immigration, President Trump and democracy. By the numbers: Democrats lead Republicans 56%-29% on the generic House ballot among 1,353 Latino registered voters in seven battleground states, according to a new bipartisan BSP Research/Shaw & Co. poll for the American Business Immigration Coalition and American Families United. Among Latino voters, Democrats lead in six states: Arizona, Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Texas. Florida breaks the pattern, with Republicans holding a 44%-43% edge. The pollsters calculated that Democrats' advantage among Latinos is 11 points wider than their Latino margin in 2024. Neither party escapes voter dissatisfaction: 39% view congressional Democrats unfavorably, compared with 63% unfavorably for congressional Republicans. State of play: Inflation and gas prices remain voters' biggest concerns, but immigration remains highly salient — though voters don't choose between enforcement and legalization as an either-or. 63% called the treatment of immigrants one of their top issues, while 59% said the same about creating legal status for undocumented immigrants with U.S.-citizen family members. 76% preferred a candidate position calling for a bipartisan path to permanent legal status and immigration reform, compared with 24% who preferred a deportation-focused position. More than 70% in every state surveyed also backed strengthening border security while providing work permits to long-term undocumented immigrants who work…

33e1d7779a:51ba17f415174c5a.title: The House left town, but Hegseth impeachment, Epstein and a funding fight are waiting
33e1d7779a:51ba17f415174c5a.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:51ba17f415174c5a.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson has sent lawmakers home until after the midterms, but when they return, they'll quickly face a showdown over impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , a renewed Epstein files fight and a looming government funding deadline. Why it matters: None of these issues will be easy to resolve and could create a headache for the Trump administration in a lame-duck session after Election Day. Driving the news: Johnson's early seven-week recess sidestepped internal warfare but guaranteed a chaotic stretch of headline-generating fights when lawmakers return. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced a resolution Tuesday to impeach Hegseth, allowing him to force the House to act on it when lawmakers return. Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) also say they now have enough lawmakers committed to signing a petition to force another vote on files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein . And government funding expires Dec. 11, giving lawmakers only about a month after they return to resolve another funding fight before the holidays. Between the lines: The midterms will determine who controls the next Congress. While Republicans remain in charge regardless of election results until Jan. 3, a Democratic-controlled House would end unified Republican control of Washington and gain control of the House agenda. The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. What they're saying: A spokesperson for Johnson referred Axios to his Wednesday comments defending the schedule change so members could "go home to their districts and make their case to the American people." Johnson called the idea the House adjourned to avoid a Hegseth impeachment vote "ridiculous" and dismissed Massie's resolution as a "publicity stunt by someone who wants attention." Hegseth, Johnson said, has "done an extraordinary job." Yes, but: If Republicans keep the House and Senate, the GOP will be expected to follow through on President Trump's promise to…

33e1d7779a:ea817bb0c169f857.title: Khanna, Massie say they can force another Epstein vote
33e1d7779a:ea817bb0c169f857.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:ea817bb0c169f857.summary: Reps. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Thomas Massie (R-Ky. ) announced Thursday they've secured commitments for the 218 signatures needed to force another vote the release of files related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein . The big picture: Answers about the disgraced financier and his web of wealthy connections have continued to haunt the administration, with Attorney General Todd Blanche now facing the threat of contempt proceedings over the Epstein files. This is the bipartisan duo's second push in less than a year after they forced their first Epstein transparency bill through Congress, which the president signed after initially opposing the effort. Driving the news: " Thomas Massie and I have defied history for a second time," Khanna said in a video posted to social media late Thursday afternoon. His post read that the pair had secured commitments for 218 votes on their discharge petition, including from three Republicans: Reps. Ralph Norman (R-S.C), Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) and Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.). Two Democrats were sick, he added, but will sign the day the House returns. Massie also posted that he and his partner across the aisle would have enough names once lawmakers are back from a lengthy recess. Friction point: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) dumped fuel on the fire blazing between him and Massie by again sending the House home early this week, Axios' Kate Santaliz reports. The more than six-week recess will also delay Massie's effort to force a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Johnson's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. What's inside: Massie and Khanna introduced the Epstein Files Transparency Act II in July to strengthen enforcement of last year's law. It would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the U.S. attorney general over alleged unlawful withholdings, redactions or failure to produce records. The bill would also require the attorney general provide certain unredacted…

33e1d7779a:8ca764ff78e4a2da.title: Why Sydney Sweeney's nude ad struck such a nerve with women athletes
33e1d7779a:8ca764ff78e4a2da.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:8ca764ff78e4a2da.summary: A sports-betting ad featuring a semi-nude Sydney Sweeney triggered a backlash across women's sports , with female athletes flooding social media with a countermessage: This is what women in sports actually look like. The big picture: Ads have long sexualized women, but the Novig ad's appeal to the male gaze hit differently at a moment when female athletes have cultural cachet and the platforms to push back. Driving the news: Highlight reels of women diving , pitching , tackling , shredding , lifting , skating , sprinting , leaping and covering sports have flooded social media this week — all with the same core message. British sprinter Amy Hunt delivered that refrain on-air this week, smiling and out of breath after the World Athletics Ultimate Championship: "Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like: 21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears," referring to American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's winning time . Women's sports are in an era of rapid momentum: The NCAA reported record high women's participation earlier this year, while Bank of America predicted U.S. women's sports revenue will grow more than 250% by 2030. There's still a long way to go on screen time, says Purdue University professor Cheryl Cooky, who studies sports and gender. But she says traditional media increasingly covers women's sports more seriously. Still, Cooky says , "it's in some ways not surprising that we get [the] Sydney Sweeney ad at this moment," describing it as "part of a backlash to the kinds of gains that women's sports, and by proxy, women more generally, are making in our society." Some online argued the ad wasn't meant to portray a female athlete and was instead targeting sports bettors, who are more likely to be men. But Cooky says it still struck a nerve because "we thought we were past the point of having to make a case that women in sport contexts are not simply sexual objects for male consumption." Between the lines: Even if traditional media has made…

33e1d7779a:7b9978e96806ff7f.summary: Warren Buffett will step down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, less than a year after handing over the CEO reins, the company said Friday.
